title: LNER's on-train AIVR camera AI flags a minor track fault near Retford a week after a driver-reported defect cost 10,000 delay minutes; overnight repair, zero delay minutes
summary: New Civil Engineer (6 Jul 2026) quoting LNER's 9 Apr 2026 announcement: after a January 2026 Cambridgeshire defect caused over 10,000 delay minutes, One Big Circle's AIVR identified a developing fa...
account: New Civil Engineer's Tom Pashby reported on 6 Jul 2026. His story was about the system flagging a snake as a track defect on 3 July. LNER runs the Pantograph Damage Assessment System (PANDAS) and One Big Circle's Automated Intelligent Video Review (AIVR) on a number of its trains. They assess overhead line equipment and track and report potential damage to Network Rail. The article reproduces LNER's 9 April 2026 announcement. In January 2026 a train driver in Cambridgeshire reported a track defect. It caused over 10,000 delay minutes, multiple cancellations and a full day of disruption. A week later the AIVR system identified a minor fault near Retford with the potential to become a larger issue. Engineers carried out an overnight repair with no delay to passengers and zero delay minutes. An LNER spokesperson said the information is fed back to Network Rail to target areas for attention. A Network Rail spokesperson said the snake would be raised automatically as standard practice. Network Rail's own 2022 story describes AIVR as a phone-sized front-of-train device applying machine learning to video of more than 20,000 miles of track. The exact day of the Retford detection is not given. LNER's announcement itself and later Southeastern and South Western Railway AIVR releases are not among the sources.
purpose: AIVR is built to capture and analyze front-of-train video with machine learning. The aim is to find and fix track and lineside defects before they cause disruption.
